Pulumi packages come in two flavors, and each is versioned and released differently. Understanding the release artifact for each flavor is the foundation for the repository-layout advice in this guide.
The link anchors #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages exist on the packaging-components page; the private-registry and pulumi_package_publish pages exist.

Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run pulumi package publish), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
Publishing to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (e.g., v1.2.3) to the repository.

Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry; source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and ship together at the package's version.

The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
A single PulumiPlugin.yaml at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it.
The example repository layout places one PulumiPlugin.yaml at the root and components under a components/ directory.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
In the example, releasing ComponentA's enhancement bumps the package to v1.1.0 and a breaking change to ComponentB bumps it to v2.0.0, illustrating semver-consistent bumps.
The publishing-packages guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/.

A thoughtful repository strategy is essential for managing Pulumi packages at scale. Group cohesive components into one package per repository so they version and release together; use separate repositories for unrelated component groups so each package can evolve at its own pace. stances.text: Following these repository practices improves the reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed of packages an organization builds and consumes.
Pulumi recommends the strategies described for structuring Git repositories used to publish packages; following them improves reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed.

A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type; a repository with multiple packages must release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights how Pulumi consumes packages.
Pulumi recommends that a repository contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type.
Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping a cohesive set of components in that package, and using multiple repositories (one per package) for distinct packages.
The importance of the recommended repository principles grows as an organization's Pulumi adoption grows.

Using a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components is technically possible, but Pulumi does not recommend it because it forfeits meaningful semantic versioning.
